## 1. Program Overview

- **Full official program name:** Urbanized Area Formula Grants (49 U.S.C. 5307)
- **Administering federal agency:** U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT), Federal Transit Administration (FTA)[4][2].
- **Description:** The Urbanized Area Formula Grants program provides federal funding to local and regional government authorities for public transit capital investments, operating assistance, and transportation planning in urbanized areas (population 50,000+). Local governments play a central role as designated recipients or subrecipients, responsible for planning, implementing, and reporting on transit projects that address community mobility needs[4][2].

## 2. Eligible Activities

Local governments can use FTA Formula Grant funds for a range of activities, including:
- **Public transit capital investments** (e.g., purchase and overhaul of buses, trains, and related equipment)[4].
- **Planning, engineering, and design** of transit projects and technical transportation studies[4].
- **Construction and rehabilitation of transit facilities** (e.g., maintenance facilities, passenger stations)[4].
- **Implementation of complete streets and active transportation projects** that improve access to transit (e.g., sidewalks, bike lanes, ADA improvements)[4].
- **Mobility management and coordination programs** (including non-emergency medical transportation and paratransit services)[4].
- **Workforce development and training activities** for transit employees[4].
- **Crime prevention and security enhancements** for transit systems[4].

## 3. Citizen Participation Requirements

Federal regulations and FTA guidance require robust public involvement in the planning and implementation of formula grant-funded projects:
- **Public hearings and comment periods:** Local governments must hold public hearings or provide opportunities for public comment on major transit plans, service changes, and capital projects[4].
- **Community needs assessment:** Transit agencies must conduct assessments to identify and prioritize community mobility needs, often as part of the transportation planning process[2][4].
- **Resident advisory committees:** Many local governments establish citizen advisory boards or councils to provide ongoing input on transit planning and equity issues[4].
- **Annual planning/reporting with public input:** The annual and long-range transportation plans (e.g., Transportation Improvement Program, TIP) require documented public participation, including outreach to underserved and minority populations[2][4].

## 4. Leverage Points for Residents

Residents can influence local funding decisions and transit planning by:
- **Participating in public hearings and comment periods** on proposed transit projects, service changes, and funding allocations[4].
- **Engaging with resident advisory committees** or attending meetings of local transit boards or metropolitan planning organizations (MPOs)[4].
- **Providing input during community needs assessments** and surveys conducted by local transit agencies[4].
- **Contacting local government staff** such as the transit agency’s public involvement coordinator, planning department staff, or the designated recipient’s grants manager (titles may include Transit Planner, Public Engagement Officer, or Grants Administrator)[4].

## 5. Reporting & Compliance

- **Annual reporting requirements:** Local governments must submit annual reports to FTA detailing project expenditures, performance, and compliance with federal requirements[2][4].
- **Performance metrics tracked:** Metrics include ridership, service coverage, asset condition, safety incidents, and progress toward equity and accessibility goals[2][4].
- **Public availability of reports:** Annual reports, performance data, and planning documents (such as the TIP and Statewide Transportation Improvement Program, STIP) are typically made available to the public via local government or transit agency websites and at public meetings[4].

## 6. Key Resources

- **Official federal program URL:**  
  [https://www.transit.dot.gov/funding/grants/urbanized-area-formula-grants-5307](https://www.transit.dot.gov/funding/grants/urbanized-area-formula-grants-5307)[4]
- **Citizen participation plan requirements URL:**  
  [https://www.transit.dot.gov/funding/grants/grant-programs](https://www.transit.dot.gov/funding/grants/grant-programs)[5]
- **Annual allocation/formula information URL:**  
  [https://www.transit.dot.gov/funding/grants/fta-allocations-formula-and-discretionary-programs-state-fy-1998-2025](https://www.transit.dot.gov/funding/grants/fta-allocations-formula-and-discretionary-programs-state-fy-1998-2025)[9]

**Relevant federal regulations:**  
- 49 U.S.C. 5307 (Urbanized Area Formula Grants)[2][4]
- FTA Circular 9030.1E (Urbanized Area Formula Program: Program Guidance and Application Instructions)
- Public participation requirements are further detailed in FTA guidance and local MPO public participation plans.

## 1. Program Overview

- **Full official program name:** Transportation Alternatives Program (TAP), now administered as the Transportation Alternatives (TA) Set-Aside under the Surface Transportation Block Grant (STBG) Program[4][5][7].
- **Administering federal agency:** U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT), specifically the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA)[4][5][7].
- **Local government role:** Local governments are primary eligible applicants for TAP funding, responsible for proposing, developing, and implementing projects that expand transportation options for non-drivers, improve active transportation infrastructure, and enhance community quality of life[1][3][4].

## 2. Eligible Activities

Local governments can use TAP funds for a range of activities, with a focus on public transit, active transportation, complete streets, and transportation equity. Eligible activities include:

- **Construction of pedestrian and bicycle facilities** (sidewalks, bike lanes, multi-use paths)[4][5][7].
- **Safe Routes to School projects** (infrastructure and non-infrastructure to improve safety and encourage walking/biking to school)[1][4][7].
- **Conversion of abandoned railroad corridors to trails** (rail-trails)[4][7].
- **Community improvement activities** (historic preservation, vegetation management, streetscaping)[1][4].
- **Access to public transportation enhancements** (improving connections to transit stops, ADA accessibility)[4][7].
- **Complete streets planning and implementation** (designing streets for all users, including pedestrians, cyclists, and transit riders)[2][4].
- **Projects that address transportation equity** (targeting underserved or high-need communities, improving access for non-drivers)[2][7].

## 3. Citizen Participation Requirements

Federal regulations and state/local guidelines require robust citizen participation in TAP-funded projects:

- **Public hearings or comment periods:** Required as part of the project selection and planning process, often during the development of local Transportation Improvement Programs (TIPs) and Statewide TIPs (STIPs)[3][8].
- **Community needs assessment:** Many states and MPOs require applicants to demonstrate community support and conduct needs assessments, often through surveys, workshops, or public meetings[3][8].
- **Resident advisory committees or councils:** Some local governments establish advisory committees to review proposals and provide input on project priorities[3].
- **Annual planning or reporting with public input:** The annual planning process for TIPs/STIPs and periodic program evaluations require opportunities for public comment and engagement[3][8].

## 4. Leverage Points for Residents

Residents can influence local TAP funding decisions through several avenues:

- **Participate in public meetings and hearings** held by local governments, MPOs, or state DOTs during project selection and planning[3][8].
- **Submit comments during open comment periods** for TIPs, STIPs, or specific TAP project proposals[3][8].
- **Join or engage with resident advisory committees** or local advocacy groups focused on transportation, biking, walking, or equity[3].
- **Contact local government staff** such as transportation planners, public works directors, or the designated TAP program coordinator to express support or concerns about specific projects[3][4].
- **Monitor local government and MPO websites** for announcements of funding cycles, application deadlines, and opportunities for input[3][4].

## 5. Reporting & Compliance

- **Annual reporting requirements:** States and MPOs must report annually to FHWA on the use of TAP funds, including project status and expenditures[8].
- **Performance metrics tracked:** Metrics may include miles of new sidewalks/bike lanes, number of Safe Routes to School projects, improvements in access to transit, and measures of community impact or equity[2][8].
- **Public availability of reports:** Annual reports and project lists are typically published on state DOT, MPO, or local government websites, and are available for public review[3][8].

## 6. Key Resources

- **Official federal program URL:**  
  [https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/environment/transportation_alternatives/](https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/environment/transportation_alternatives/)[7]
- **Citizen participation plan requirements URL:**  
  [https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/environment/transportation_alternatives/guidance/guidance_2022.cfm](https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/environment/transportation_alternatives/guidance/guidance_2022.cfm)[8]
- **Annual allocation/formula information URL:**  
  [https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/bipartisan-infrastructure-law/ta.cfm](https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/bipartisan-infrastructure-law/ta.cfm)[7]

**Note:** For specific regulatory requirements, see 23 U.S.C. 133(h) (federal statute for TA Set-Aside) and FHWA guidance documents[8]. Local implementation may also reference 23 CFR Part 450 for metropolitan and statewide planning requirements.
